steps: Remove and destroy all heavily spotted or yellowed leaves immediately.
Water your plants at the base only — do not wet the leaves.
Space plants further apart so air can move between them freely.
Place a layer of mulch around the base of each plant to stop soil from splashing up.
Check remaining plants every 2–3 days and remove any newly affected leaves.
escalate_if: Spots spread to more than 30% of the plant
Symptoms appear on fruits as well as leaves
Disease continues spreading after one week of management

steps: Immediately remove and burn all infected leaves, stems, and fruit — do not leave them in the field.
Stop all overhead watering. Water only at the base of each plant.
Ensure water does not stand in or around the field — improve drainage if needed.
Do not walk through the field when plants are wet — this spreads the disease.
Warn nearby farmers, as this disease spreads quickly between farms.
escalate_if: Dark water-soaked patches appear on stems or fruit
White fuzzy growth is visible on the underside of leaves
Plants begin to collapse or die within days
Disease spreads to multiple plants within 24 hours

steps: Improve air movement in the growing area by removing extra leaves and opening vents if indoors.
Remove affected leaves carefully without shaking the plant — bag and dispose of them.
Water only at the base and avoid wetting the leaves at any time.
Increase the distance between plants to allow better airflow.
Clean and sanitise tools between plants to avoid spreading the mold.
escalate_if: Mold covers more than half of the leaf surface area
Yellowing spreads to new healthy leaves rapidly
Fruit production drops noticeably

steps: Remove and destroy all leaves and fruit showing dark water-soaked or raised spots.
Avoid touching healthy plants after handling infected ones — wash hands with soap.
Do not work in the field when plants are wet.
Improve drainage around each plant to reduce water splash between plants.
Clean stakes, cages, and tools used in the field with soapy water.
escalate_if: Spots appear on fruit causing large dark raised lesions
Disease spreads rapidly during rainy periods
Plants begin to shed leaves quickly

steps: Remove lower leaves with brown circular spots that have ring-like patterns inside them.
Avoid watering late in the day so leaves have time to dry before nightfall.
Do not use infected plant material as mulch or compost.
Next season, plant potato or tomato in a different part of the field.
Check the crop every 3–4 days and remove newly spotted leaves promptly.
escalate_if: Spots spread rapidly to upper leaves
Tubers show dark sunken patches after harvest
More than 40% of the plant leaves are affected

steps: Remove and destroy all above-ground infected plant parts immediately — burn or bury them deeply.
Do not leave cut or broken infected stems in the field.
If the crop is severely affected, harvest healthy tubers as soon as possible.
Store harvested tubers in a cool, dry, and well-ventilated place away from sunlight.
Inform your local agriculture officer — this is a high-risk disease that spreads quickly.
escalate_if: Dark rot is found inside harvested tubers
The entire field shows disease signs within a few days
A wet rot smell comes from soil or stored tubers

steps: Ensure the paddy field has good drainage — remove any standing water that is not needed.
Reduce nitrogen fertilizer use immediately if you recently applied a large amount.
Remove and dispose of heavily infected tillers carefully outside the field.
Maintain balanced soil nutrition — get a soil test if you can.
Keep field bunds free of weeds and crop debris.
escalate_if: Brown spots appear on the grain heads at harvest time
More than 25% of the tillers in the field show symptoms
Expected grain yield looks significantly reduced

steps: Reduce or stop applying nitrogen fertilizer immediately.
Drain the field for a few days to lower humidity at the plant level.
Remove and burn heavily infected tillers — do not leave them in the water.
In future planting, space seedlings further apart to improve airflow.
Watch the field closely every day, especially on cool and humid nights.
escalate_if: Blast lesions reach the neck of the plant — neck blast
Empty whitish grain heads appear at harvest
Large sections of the field show uniform symptoms quickly

steps: Remove lower leaves that are heavily covered with orange rust pustules.
Use drip or furrow irrigation — avoid any overhead watering.
Space plants wider apart in future seasons to allow better air movement.
Monitor young leaves closely during cool and humid weather periods.
After harvest, remove and dispose of all infected crop debris from the field.
escalate_if: Rust pustules cover more than 50% of the leaf area
Symptoms appear on husks or cobs
The entire field shows symptoms uniformly

steps: Remove infected leaves from the lower canopy early in the season.
Avoid late-season overhead watering.
In future seasons, plant in fields where corn has not been grown recently.
Increase plant spacing to reduce humidity within the crop canopy.
Clean and remove all crop residue after harvest to reduce carryover.
escalate_if: Lesions cover more than a third of the upper canopy leaves
Ear shanks and husks show symptoms
Premature plant death occurs before grain maturity

steps: Remove and destroy all leaves and fruits showing dark water-soaked spots.
Wash hands thoroughly before touching healthy plants after handling infected ones.
Avoid working in the field while plants are wet from rain or dew.
Improve field drainage to reduce water splashing between plants.
Disinfect all tools and stakes used in the field with soapy water.
escalate_if: Spots appear on fruit causing large raised dark lesions
Disease spreads rapidly during rainy periods to most plants in the field
Plants lose a large number of leaves quickly

steps: Remove and destroy all mummified berries and leaves showing brown circular spots.
Prune infected canes completely and remove them from the vineyard area.
Improve airflow through the canopy by proper training and pruning each season.
Handle fruit carefully to avoid cuts and bruises that allow infection.
Keep the ground under vines clear of fallen fruit and leaves throughout the season.
escalate_if: More than 20% of the grape cluster is shrivelled or infected
Infection appears close to harvest time
Mummified berries remain attached into the next growing season

steps: Rake and remove all fallen leaves and fruit from the ground below the tree.
Prune dense branches to open the canopy and allow sunlight and airflow inside.
Avoid wetting the leaves when watering — water at the base of the tree only.
Dispose of all infected material away from the orchard — do not compost it.
Monitor the tree closely during wet spring and early summer periods.
escalate_if: Scab lesions cover the majority of fruit surfaces
Severe defoliation occurs before mid-summer
New infections appear on current-season growth rapidly

steps: Remove all mummified fruit, cankers, and dead wood from the tree immediately.
Prune infected branches at least 15 cm below any visible wound or canker.
Rake and destroy all fallen leaves and fruit under the tree.
Avoid wounding the tree bark during pruning or harvesting.
Apply wound sealant to large pruning cuts to prevent re-entry of disease.
escalate_if: Cankers appear on the main trunk or large scaffold branches
More than 30% of fruit shows rot before or at harvest
Tree shows significant dieback of major branches
